She knew it would fail. It still took her a year to stop

The losses grew every month, and so did the messages from customers who believed in the product. Every signal said stop. She rewrote her own exit criteria three times.

Interview
Nao KurodaSCALE LLC　Co-founder
Interview & text
SECOND TAKE

In briefThe decision in three lines

  1. Revenue was growing, but few customers stayed past three months.
  2. Encouraging messages led her to move the exit line three times.
  3. She made the rule impossible to change alone — and closed the business.

Nao Kuroda wrote her own criteria for shutting the business down. Then she rewrote them. Three times.

Retention was below plan and ad spend kept climbing. At every meeting she said the next fix would turn things around. The numbers didn’t move.

It wasn’t a lack of analysis that kept her going. Behind every number, she could see the faces of the people who were counting on her.

Scene 01The warning signs came while it was growing

Which number told you the business was in trouble?

KurodaRetention. New customers kept coming, but few were still with us three months later. The revenue chart went up and to the right, but really it was a bucket with a hole in the bottom.

Did you think about shutting down then?

KurodaIntellectually, yes. But I believed that as long as we had moves left, it wasn’t a failure. Looking back, I confused having options with being able to win.

Scene 02Why the line moved three times

Why did you change the criteria you had set yourself?

KurodaEach time, something happened that looked like hope. A big inquiry, a heartfelt message from a customer. The numbers stayed bad, but the story kept going.

Support can carry a new venture. It can also cloud judgment. Kuroda was stuck between wanting to live up to her customers’ hopes and her responsibility to the company as a whole.

KurodaI thought continuing was the honest thing to do. Really, I was just putting off the pain of deciding.

Scene 03The day she stopped looking for reasons to continue

What finally made you decide?

KurodaMy co-founder asked me, “If we hadn’t started this yet and you saw these numbers today — would you start it?” The answer was no.

Trying to protect the time and money already spent drags every future decision back into the past. The next day, Kuroda began explaining the decision to customers, arranging refunds and finding them somewhere else to go.

Scene 04One promise for the next venture

What will you do differently when you start the next one?

KurodaI’ll make the exit line a promise to the team, not to myself. Nobody can change it alone, and the decision date goes in the calendar on day one. On the days I’m most excited, I want the rules my calm self wrote to still be there.
